extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / readers of the Philosophical Transactions (17th‑century scientific community)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing observational natural‑history and related scientific reports (including book reviews and experimental notes) that record measurements, locality, comparison to prior authorities, and reasoning. Emphasizes precise timings, descriptions, experimental detail, and practical/mathematical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise temporal and positional measurement of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record exact times and positions for astronomical events and other observations (e.g. 'September 8, 1671, at 7 h. 27-l-m. I first observed the moon eclipsed...', and for sunspots: 'Sept. 1, at three o'clock, I saw the same spot moved about a quarter of the diameter of the sun westward').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give clock times (hours, minutes, seconds or fractions), measure angular distances (fractions of the sun's diameter, distance from limb), and repeat measurements to check exactness. Multiple timed observations allow calculation of apparent velocities and periods (as with sunspots leading to an inferred ~27.1 day period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated observations and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Make repeated observations and measurements to establish accuracy (e.g. 'I examined and measured several times, and found very exact' for a sunspot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-observe phenomena across times/days to confirm motion/changes; use repeats to detect observational errors and to infer periodicities or trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail morphological description and apparent changes with viewing geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the shape, size, and apparent changes of phenomena with position (e.g. sunspot described as 'one greater and two lesser black spots with a dusky cloud encompassing them'; notes that the spot's apparent diameter in one axis shortens near the limb due to optics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record both intrinsic appearance and how apparent form changes with angle or optical projection; explain apparent distortions by geometric/optical reasoning when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and rule out confounders (environmental/atmospheric conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note conditions that might affect observation and explicitly rule them out when unjustified (e.g. 'It did not seem to be caused by any clouds or exhalations in the air, the sky near the moon being very clear').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document sky/cloud cover, seeing conditions, and any factors that could produce spurious effects; discuss whether such factors could explain observed phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative inference from observations (periods, velocities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use measured temporal/positional data to infer quantitative properties like apparent velocity or rotation period (e.g. from sunspot motion infer 'apparent periodical revolution about the sun's axis, about 27-1 days').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the hypothesis linking measurements to the inferred quantity and the assumptions involved (e.g. assuming spots adhere to the solar surface); show arithmetic or reasoning connecting observations to the inferred value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide plausible causal hypotheses and discuss alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer causes for observed phenomena and consider alternatives (e.g. suggests lunar penumbral colours might be 'caused by the refraction of the light from the sun through the atmosphere about the earth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State hypotheses cautiously, relate them to observations, and discuss other possible explanations; avoid dogmatic claims without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locality, provenance, and specimen context for natural objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the exact provenance and geological/locational context of specimens (e.g. quarry names, counties: 'Adderton in Yorkshire', 'Wansford ... Northamptonshire'; 'found in a sandy ditch bank about a mile and a half from York').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give specific locality data and the substrate or matrix in which specimens occur; compare occurrences across localities to assess whether specimens are indigenous or reworked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare specimens with living analogues and with surrounding matrix
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare fossil/resembling specimens to living species and to the rock that contains them (e.g. argument that English quarry 'cockle-like stones' 'have no parts of a different texture from the rock' and thus 'never were any part of an animal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine texture/composition differences (or lack thereof) between fossils and host rock; search for matching living species in nearby habitats; use negative searches (not finding living analogues) as part of reasoning, with appropriate caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state methods, procedures and negative results
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe methods used and report negative or failed attempts (e.g. 'I put it into a box, expecting it would have produced an ichneumon, but it dried away and nothing came of it').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document how specimens/experiments were handled, the procedures followed, and any outcomes including failures; negative results are evidence and should be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite, compare with, and where necessary dissent from prior authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference earlier works and explain agreements or differences in view (e.g. engages Steno's Prodromus on petrified shells and explains differences are from 'a different view of nature', transcribes classical authors regarding ichneumons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how new observations align or conflict with earlier claims; reproduce key passages when relevant and explain reasons for disagreement without ad hominem dismissals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experiments and comparative trials to resolve controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve debated points with experiments/comparisons (e.g. accounts of vipers' venom experiments where multiple animals were bitten in sequence to test transmissibility of venom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and report experiments that address the central claim, include controls where feasible, and describe outcomes and their interpretation; note limitations (geographic/species differences) affecting generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize descriptive works for practical utility (systematic arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange material so it is useful to practitioners (e.g. botanical work arranged alphabetically by four seasons to know when to gather plants; naval architecture divided into detailed chapters with proportions, diagrams, and rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose organization that aids usability: seasonal, functional, or stepwise structures; include indices, chapter divisions, and cross‑references to facilitate use in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include diagrams, measures, and mathematical/physical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Support textual description with diagrams, measures and quantitative/mathematical explanation (e.g. Wallis's treatise includes 'methods of computing the weight sustained by every joint', 'measure of the length of the spiral line', and explanations for why certain hull shapes perform better).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide figures, worked calculations, dimensional specifications and derivations that justify practical recommendations; state assumptions and units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness and breadth balanced with relevance to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess works for how exhaustively they treat a subject and whether that treatment serves the intended readers (e.g. a pharmaceutical treatise is judged 'not be interesting to the medical reader of the present day'; Witsen's naval work is praised for its ample seaman's dictionary and diagrams).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing or composing a work, evaluate whether scope, depth, and detail match contemporary needs; comment on parts likely to interest practitioners vs antiquarian or historical digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report observational particulars down to small details and sensory notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Include small but relevant sensory details and specimen descriptions (e.g. color, smell: 'those without wings were of a light yellow... emitted an acid or sour scent; those with wings were coal black... emitted a smell like musk').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe colour, smell, texture, and condition of specimens, noting sex differences or life‑cycle states when observed; such details can be diagnostic or suggest biological functions (e.g. scent during coitus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make cautious etiological claims when direct evidence is lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence is indirect, qualify assertions and suggest further inquiry (e.g. 'I am apt to think there is no such matter as petrifying of shells in the business... but that these cockle-like stones ever were, as they are at present, lapides sui generis').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase conclusions with appropriate hedging; recommend further observations, experiments, or correspondents' input to resolve uncertainties.
